name: Androstenedione
lead: Androstenedione (androst-4-ene-3,17-dione, often called "andro" or A4) is an endogenous steroid hormone made in the adrenal glands and gonads. It is a weak androgen and an intermediate in the body's synthesis of testosterone and of estrone, and it can be converted in either direction between itself and testosterone [1][2]. Its level in blood is used as a marker in conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome and congenital adrenal hyperplasia [3][4].

In the 1990s it was sold in the United States as an over-the-counter dietary supplement promoted as a testosterone booster for strength and muscle, and became widely known through its use by professional baseball players [5][1]. Controlled studies in men reported that low doses did not raise testosterone meaningfully, and a review found no improvement in strength, muscle size or body fat at 50 to 100 mg per day [5]. It is now a Schedule III controlled substance in the US and is banned in most organised sport [5].

paras: Androstenedione is produced mainly in the adrenal cortex, the ovarian theca cells and the testicular Leydig cells. It is formed from 17-hydroxyprogesterone or from DHEA and can be reduced to testosterone or aromatized to estrone [1][2]. Women secrete more androgen than estrogen by quantity, with androstenedione among the main circulating androgens, though it binds the androgen receptor only weakly [4]. In men, Leydig cell androgen production is regulated by luteinizing hormone [2].

Androstenedione was marketed as a precursor that the body would convert to testosterone. Sports Illustrated credits Patrick Arnold with introducing it to the North American market, and players such as Mark McGwire used it in Major League Baseball in the 1990s [5]. In the 2000s it was sold under the same name and, after bans, as related products; T Nation members note that products marketed as 1-andro followed after androstenedione and related compounds were restricted [6].

A 2000 JAMA study by Leder and colleagues found that a single 300 mg oral dose raised testosterone in men over eight hours, whereas 100 mg did not produce a significant change; estradiol rose at both doses and responses varied between individuals [5]. A 2006 review by Brown and colleagues concluded that 50 to 100 mg per day did not improve muscle strength, muscle size or body fat, and that one study using 300 mg daily with other supplements also showed no strength gain. The reviewers suggested higher doses had not been shown to work and advised against use [5].

A study in ten healthy women given 100 mg reported masculinising effects, menstrual disturbances and metabolic changes [5]. The remaining published literature on androstenedione concerns its role as a hormone in other conditions, such as polycystic ovary syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and breast cancer risk, and not use as a supplement [3][4][7][8].

Because androstenedione is converted to both testosterone and estrogens, reviews and users have raised concerns about estrogenic effects such as gynecomastia in men, lipid changes and suppression of natural testosterone [5][9]. In women, the 100 mg study reported voice deepening, hirsutism, clitoral enlargement and menstrual irregularity [5]. Observational studies link higher endogenous levels of androgens and estrogens to breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women, but these studies concern the body's own hormones and not supplements [7].

The International Olympic Committee banned androstenedione as an anabolic steroid in 1997 [5]. Through the late 1990s the White House drug policy director concluded that it could not be classed as an anabolic steroid without proof it built muscle [5]. The FDA banned its sale as a supplement on 11 April 2004, and the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004, effective January 2005, made it a Schedule III controlled substance [5]. It is banned by WADA, MLB, the NFL, the NBA, the NCAA and the US military [5].

Current community discussion is limited. T Nation users refer to it as a weak androgen and a DHEA metabolite no longer sold as a supplement, discuss it in lab panels for post-cycle hormone testing, and cite it in explanations of hormone pathways [9][10][11]. The Grokipedia article summarises supplement use as promoted for performance in the 1990s with limited evidence of efficacy [12].

lore.intro: Androstenedione appears in T Nation threads mostly as a hormone-pathway topic and as a historical prohormone [6][9][10].

claims.claim: Oral androstenedione converts to testosterone and builds muscle
claims.believers: Marketing in the 1990s promoted it as a testosterone precursor; forum users note the interconversion of the two hormones [5][13].
claims.experts: A 2006 review found 50 to 100 mg per day did not improve strength, muscle size or body fat, and a 2000 study saw testosterone rise only at a 300 mg single dose, with higher estradiol [5].

claims.claim: It is a weak androgen with mostly estrogenic downsides
claims.believers: A T Nation poster described it as a weak androgen and DHEA metabolite and said it was no longer favoured for these reasons [9].
claims.experts: It is described in reviews as a weak androgen and an aromatase substrate that gives rise to estrone [1][5].

claims.claim: Banned prohormones were replaced by relabelled analogues such as 1-andro
claims.believers: A T Nation user said it was marketed as 1-andro after androstenedione and analogues were banned [6].
claims.experts: Regulators extended controls through the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004; no trials of the replacement products are cited here [5].

card.summary: A weak natural androgen once sold as the 90s baseball-era testosterone-booster supplement; trials found no strength or muscle gains at ordinary doses.
card.note: US Schedule III since 2005; banned in sport; estrogenic and androgenic side effects reported.

quick.overview:
Androstenedione is a hormone the body makes as a step toward testosterone and estrogen. In the 1990s it was sold as a supplement that would raise testosterone and build muscle, and became famous through baseball.

Controlled studies found that ordinary doses did not improve strength, muscle size or fat, and a single large dose raised testosterone only briefly while also raising estradiol.
quick.mechanism: It is converted by enzymes to testosterone, or by aromatase to estrone. It is itself only a weak androgen, so any effect depends on how much converts.
quick.risks: The 100 mg study in women reported masculinising effects and menstrual disruption. Estrogenic effects are a concern in men. It was banned as a supplement in 2004 and has been a Schedule III controlled substance in the US since 2005; it is banned in major sports.
